slides.title: log
speaker_notes: Welcome to Section 4.3 on Logarithmic Functions.
This section introduces logarithms as the INVERSE of exponential functions. The key idea: if b^x = y, then log_b(y) = x.
Prerequisites: Students should be comfortable with exponential functions from Section 4.2, including properties of f(x) = b^x and the natural base e.
Key theme: Logarithms answer the question 'What exponent do I need?' This is the fundamental shift students need to grasp.

slides.title: LEARNING OBJECTIVES
text: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
Convert between logarithmic and exponential forms
Evaluate logarithmic expressions (including common and natural logs)
Graph logarithmic functions and identify key features
speaker_notes: Read objectives aloud. Emphasize that logarithms are the INVERSE of exponential functions — they 'undo' exponentiation.
Objective 1 (converting forms) is the most foundational skill. Everything else builds on it.
Objective 6 (solving equations) connects directly to Sections 4.4-4.5 where we solve more complex log/exp equations.

slides.title: REVIEW: INVERSE FUNCTIONS
text: Before we define logarithms, recall the concept of an inverse function:
The inverse of a function undoes what the function does. If f assigns y to x, then f ⁻¹ assigns x back to y.
g(f(x)) = x for all x in domain of f
f(g(x)) = x for all x in domain of g
The exponential function f(x) = bx is one-to-one, so it has an inverse: f ⁻¹(x) = logb(x).
speaker_notes: QUICK REVIEW: Ask students 'If f(x) = 2x + 1, what does f⁻¹ do?'
Answer: f⁻¹ subtracts 1 then divides by 2 (undoes the operations in reverse).
The key connection: The exponential function f(x) = bˣ is one-to-one (passes the horizontal line test), so it HAS an inverse.
That inverse is what we call the logarithmic function.
Example with numbers: If f(x) = 2ˣ, then f(3) = 8. The inverse asks: '2 raised to WHAT power gives 8?' Answer: 3. So log₂(8) = 3.

slides.title: DEFINITION
text: If x and b are positive real numbers such that b ≠ 1, then the logarithmic function with base b is:
𝒚 = 𝑙𝑜𝑔𝑏(𝑥) is equivalent to 𝒃𝒚 = 𝒙
speaker_notes: KEY DEFINITION — This is the most important slide in the section.
Say it clearly: 'log base b of x equals y' means 'b raised to the y power equals x.'
The logarithm IS an exponent. log₂(8) = 3 because 2³ = 8.
Why b > 0 and b ≠ 1? Same reasons as exponential functions — negative bases cause problems, and base 1 gives a constant.
Why x > 0? Because bʸ is always positive for b > 0, so we can only take logarithms of positive numbers.
COMMON CONFUSION: Students mix up which number is the base, which is the exponent, and which is the result. Use color-coding on the board.

slides.title: TRY IT: CONVERT TO EXPONENTIAL FORM
text: Write each logarithmic equation in exponential form.
Pause and try this before advancing!
speaker_notes: Give students 2-3 minutes.
HINTS if students are stuck:
• 'The logarithm IS the exponent.'
• 'log base b of x = y means b^y = x'
• For (d): recall that ln means log base e.
COMMON MISTAKES:
• Writing 64³ = 4 (confusing base and result)
• Not knowing that ln = log base e

slides.title: SOLUTION: CONVERT TO EXPONENTIAL FORM
text: Remember: logb(x) = y means by = x. The logarithm is always the exponent!
speaker_notes: Walk through each conversion. Emphasize the pattern:
• The base of the log becomes the base of the exponential
• The answer (right side of log equation) becomes the exponent
• The argument of the log becomes the result
For (d), stress that ln = log_e. This trips students up constantly.
Verification strategy: Always check by computing the exponential side.

slides.title: TRY IT: CONVERT TO LOGARITHMIC FORM
text: Write each exponential equation in logarithmic form.
Pause and try this before advancing!
speaker_notes: This is the reverse of the previous exercise. Students should identify:
• The base stays the same
• The exponent becomes the answer of the log
• The result becomes the argument of the log
Watch for: Students writing log₁₂₅(5) = 3 instead of log₅(125) = 3 — they swap the base and argument.

slides.title: SOLUTION: CONVERT TO LOGARITHMIC FORM
text: As a function: f(x) = log4(x) For example, f(1/64) = −3 because 4−3 = 1/64.
speaker_notes: Emphasize the conversion pattern:
b^y = x → log_b(x) = y
For (c): Point out that log₁₀ is the 'common log' and is written simply as 'log' (no base shown).
For (d): log_e is the 'natural log' and is written as 'ln'.
Ask: 'What does log₅(125) = 3 MEAN in words?' Answer: '5 raised to the 3rd power equals 125.'

slides.title: EVALUATING LOGARITHMIC EXPRESSIONS
text: To evaluate logb(x), ask: "b raised to what power gives x?"
speaker_notes: Work through each example step by step. The key strategy is always the same:
1. Set up: log_b(x) = ?
2. Convert: b^? = x
3. Ask: what exponent works?
For Example 3: Students need to recognize √5 = 5^(1/2).
For Example 4: log_b(1) = 0 for ANY base b because b⁰ = 1 always.

slides.title: COMMON AND NATURAL LOGARITHMS
text: Base 10 is the default — when you see "log"
with no base written, it means base 10.
Your calculator's LOG button is base 10.
Base e ≈ 2.71828 — the natural base from
Your calculator's LN button is base e.
speaker_notes: Two special bases built into every calculator:
1. Common Log (base 10): Written as 'log' with no subscript. Your LOG key.
2. Natural Log (base e): Written as 'ln'. Your LN key.
IMPORTANT: All other bases require the change-of-base formula (coming later).
Demonstrate on calculator:

slides.title: TRY IT: EVALUATE WITH A CALCULATOR
text: Use your calculator. Round to 4 decimal places. Check using exponential form.
Pause and try this before advancing!
speaker_notes: CALCULATOR KEYSTROKES:
• log(0.015): LOG 0.015 ENTER → −1.8239 (negative because 0.015 < 1)
• ln(1): LN 1 ENTER → 0 (property: ln(1) = 0 always)

slides.title: SOLUTION: EVALUATE WITH A CALCULATOR
text: Check: e0 = 1 ✓ (No calculator needed! logb(1) = 0 for any base)
speaker_notes: Key takeaways:
1. log(x) positive when x > 1, zero when x = 1, negative when 0 < x < 1.
2. ln(x) same pattern.
3. Always verify by converting back to exponential form.
4. ln(1) = 0 is a property — no calculator needed.

slides.title: BASIC PROPERTIES OF LOGARITHMS
text: These properties come directly from the definition. They are used constantly in solving equations!
speaker_notes: Five foundational properties:
1. log_b(1) = 0 — log of 1 is ALWAYS 0
2. log_b(b) = 1 — log of the base is ALWAYS 1
3. log_b(b^x) = x — log and exp are inverses
4. b^(log_b(x)) = x — other direction of inverse
5. One-to-One — equal logs (same base) → equal arguments
Quick drill: log₇(1)? → 0. log₅(5)? → 1. ln(e³)? → 3. 10^(log 50)? → 50.

slides.title: TRY IT: SIMPLIFY USING PROPERTIES
text: Simplify each expression without a calculator.
Pause and try this before advancing!
speaker_notes: 3-4 minutes. All done WITHOUT a calculator.
(d) b^(log_b x) = x → 12. (e) log_b(b^x) = x → 3. (f) e^(ln x) = x → 7.

slides.title: SOLUTION: SIMPLIFY USING PROPERTIES
text: All follow directly from the basic properties. No calculator needed!
speaker_notes: Review each answer. The inverse properties (c-f) are the most important for solving equations later.

slides.title: GRAPHS OF LOGARITHMIC FUNCTIONS
text: Since f(x) = logb(x) is the inverse of g(x) = bx, their graphs are reflections across y = x.
Rewrite as 2y = x and choose y-values:
Tip: Choose y-values first, then compute x = 2y. Avoids fractions!
Inverse functions swap domain/range, x/y-intercepts, and horizontal/vertical asymptotes!
speaker_notes: GRAPHING TIP: To graph y = log_b(x), rewrite as b^y = x. Pick nice y-values and compute x.
Emphasize the INVERSE RELATIONSHIP — everything swaps:
• domain ↔ range
• x-int ↔ y-int
• horizontal asymptote ↔ vertical asymptote

slides.title: PROPERTIES OF f(x) = logb(x)
text: Both cases: Domain: (0, ∞) Range: (−∞, ∞) x-intercept: (1, 0) Asymptote: x = 0
Graph rises slowly to the right
Graph falls slowly to the right
Key Question: How do you tell growth from decay? Look at the base b, same as with exponentials!
speaker_notes: BIG PICTURE: b > 1 → increasing, 0 < b < 1 → decreasing. Both share domain (0,∞), range (−∞,∞), x-int (1,0), asymptote x = 0.

slides.title: TRY IT: GRAPH A LOGARITHMIC FUNCTION
text: Graph f(x) = log2(x + 1) + 2. Identify the domain, range, and vertical asymptote.
Hint: Start with the parent function y = log2(x). How does it shift?
Pause and try this before advancing!
speaker_notes: Students should recognize: parent y = log₂(x), (x+1) shifts LEFT 1, +2 shifts UP 2.
Asymptote: x = −1. Domain: (−1, ∞). Range: (−∞, ∞).

slides.title: SOLUTION: GRAPH f(x) = log2(x + 1) + 2
speaker_notes: Walk through each computation. y-intercept: f(0) = log₂(1) + 2 = 0 + 2 = 2. x-intercept: set f(x) = 0 → log₂(x+1) = −2 → x+1 = 1/4 → x = −3/4.

slides.title: DOMAIN OF LOGARITHMIC FUNCTIONS
text: The argument of a logarithm must be strictly positive. For f(x) = logb(g(x)), the domain requires g(x) > 0.
Find boundary points, test intervals. Vertical asymptotes at x = −2 and x = 2.
speaker_notes: DOMAIN: Set argument > 0 and solve. Example 2 shows the domain can be all reals. Example 3 requires factoring and sign analysis.

slides.title: SOLVING LOGARITHMIC EQUATIONS
text: Strategy: Convert to exponential form or use the one-to-one property.
speaker_notes: Three strategies:
1. CONVERT TO EXPONENTIAL — single log = number.
2. ONE-TO-ONE — log_b(A) = log_b(B) → A = B.
3. INVERSE PROPERTIES — e^(ln x) = x, 10^(log x) = x.
Always check: log arguments must be positive!

slides.title: TRY IT: SOLVE LOGARITHMIC EQUATIONS
text: c) logx(232) = 21 (solve for x, round to 3 dec.)
Pause and try this before advancing!
speaker_notes: 5 minutes. (a) One-to-one, (b) Take ln of both sides, (c) Convert to exponential, (d) Take log of both sides.

slides.title: SOLUTION: SOLVE LOGARITHMIC EQUATIONS
text: Verify all log arguments remain positive. Extraneous solutions can arise with logarithms.
speaker_notes: (a) One-to-one. (b) ln both sides. (c) Convert to exponential. (d) Take log both sides = change of base.

slides.title: CHANGE-OF-BASE FORMULA
text: Your calculator only has LOG (base 10) and LN (base e). To evaluate other bases, convert!
"To convert from base a, divide by log(a)."
speaker_notes: This formula solves: 'My calculator can't do log₃(x)!' Use log(x)/log(a) or ln(x)/ln(a).
Verification: 4^2.322 ≈ 25 ✓

slides.title: TRY IT: CHANGE-OF-BASE FORMULA
text: Evaluate using change-of-base. Round to 3 decimal places.
Pause and try this before advancing!

slides.title: SOLUTION: CHANGE-OF-BASE FORMULA
speaker_notes: Both log and ln give the same final answer. Use whichever is more convenient.

slides.title: APPLICATION: STAR MAGNITUDE
text: Astronomers use logarithmic scales to measure star brightness.
M = absolute magnitude m = apparent magnitude d = distance in parsecs
speaker_notes: Logarithmic scales in action. The Sun appears very bright (m = −26.74) only because it's close. Its absolute magnitude (4.83) is actually average.

slides.title: COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID
text: The log of a SUM is NOT the sum of logs. #1 mistake. (logb(xy) = logb(x) + logb(y) IS true — Product Rule in 4.4.)
You can only take log of a POSITIVE number. log(0) and log(−5) are undefined. Always check solutions!
In logb(x) = y: b is the base, x is the argument, y is the exponent. Convert: by = x (not xy = b).
log2(8) ≠ log · 2 · 8. The subscript 2 is the BASE. log2(8) = 3 because 23 = 8.
When solving log equations, ALWAYS verify answers don't make any argument ≤ 0. Reject any that do.
speaker_notes: The #1 mistake: distributing log over addition. Emphasize: log(a+b) ≠ log(a)+log(b). But log(ab) = log(a)+log(b) IS correct (Product Rule, Section 4.4).

slides.title: KEY TAKEAWAYS
text: The logarithm IS the exponent. Converting between forms is the fundamental skill.
Common log = log10, Natural log = ln = loge
These are the only two bases on your calculator. All others need change of base.
Plus the inverse property blog_b(x) = x and the one-to-one property.
Domain of logb(x) is (0, ∞) — argument must be positive
Vertical asymptote at x = 0. Graph passes through (1, 0). Inverse of bx.
Change of base: loga(x) = log(x)/log(a) = ln(x)/ln(a)
Use this to evaluate any log with your calculator.
speaker_notes: WRAP-UP. Looking ahead: Section 4.4 covers Product/Quotient/Power Rules. Section 4.5 covers full exponential and logarithmic equations.
